doc.title: Hal Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Hearing Ben Pollack in 1964 and older drummers' set-ups
summary: He heard Pollack's band at the first festival he attended and recalls it in retrospect.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: The first jazz festival I went to was Dixieland at Disneyland, in 1964, and Pollock had a band there. And through suppressed memory, now I remember what he sounded like. At the time it was too much for me to absorb but thinking back on it I’m remembering the details of what he played. And the more I hear him on recordings and tape I remember what he did.
Some of those guys didn’t even — they had a different way of setting up their drums, didn’t they?

They sure did, yeah. The older players tended to use larger bass drums, and maybe two tom-toms. Floor tom, two mounted toms, wood block, two cowbells, and the cymbals down low, snare drum toted way over, which is a hold over from marching bands, when it’s slung over your shoulder you play like you would in a military band. But all the Chicago drummers learned rudiments and classical technique from drummers who had come out of that military and classical tradition. So they played like that and lifted their sticks way high off the drum and all that. And I still tilt mine over, it’s much easier to play. I can’t play it the other way now.
Do you recall seeing — I think it’s the Glenn Miller movie, and Ben Pollack is in it?
Sure is, and the Benny Goodman Story too.

And he plays closed rolls and the hi-hat. Yeah. I remember him doing that. And a stick on the bass drum. That’s a technique you don’t see too much anymore. Keep a four beat going on the bass drum and play a little syncopation against it with either the left or the right stick. I’d do that this weekend but with that 18-inch bass drum I’ll drop a stick reaching for it.
